summary.text: For every prime \(p\), only \(1\) and \(p\) have all their prime factors among those of \(p\), so \(a(p)\le 2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and an arbitrarily large prime \(p\ge 81\) gives \(\sqrt{\log p}>2\), contradicting the asserted eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime divisor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
(For \(k=1\), the set of prime divisors is empty, so \(1\) is always counted.) We disprove the proposed assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
The obstruction is supplied by arbitrarily large prime values of \(n\).

First observe that if \(p\) is prime, then
\[
a(p)=2.
\]
Indeed, the prime divisors of \(p\) form the singleton set \(\{p\}\). Both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted: \(1\) has no prime divisors, while the only prime divisor of \(p\) is \(p\) itself. Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) is counted. If \(k=1\), it is one of the two numbers already listed. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has some prime divisor \(q\). Because \(k\) is counted, every prime divisor of \(k\) must divide \(p\), and since \(p\) is prime this forces \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). A positive multiple of \(p\) which is at most \(p\) must equal \(p\), so \(k=p\). Hence there are no further counted numbers and \(a(p)=2\) (the weaker inequality \(a(p)\le2\) would already suffice).

Now choose the particular exponent parameter
\[
\epsilon=\frac12.
\]
Assume, for contradiction, that the conjectured assertion holds. Since \(\epsilon>0\), there is then an integer \(N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a prime
\[
p\ge \max\{N,81\}.
\]
Such a prime exists because primes are unbounded. For completeness, unboundedness follows from Euclid's argument: given any bound \(B\), the integer \(B!+1>1\) has a prime divisor \(p\); no prime at most \(B\) can divide \(B!+1\), since it divides \(B!\), so this prime divisor satisfies \(p>B\). Applying this with a bound at least \(\max\{N,81\}\) produces the required prime (and a strict inequality is more than is needed).

Because \(p\ge N\), the asserted eventual lower bound applies to \(p\), giving
\[
\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.
\]
We show that the opposite strict inequality holds.

First, \(e<3\). One elementary justification is the exponential series
\[
e=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
  =2+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}.
\]
For \(j\ge2\), one has \(j!\ge 2^{j-1}\), and the inequality is strict for every \(j\ge3\). Consequently
\[
\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
 <\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{j-1}}=1,
\]
so indeed \(e<3\). Since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive reals,
\[
1=\log e<\log 3.
\]
Using \(81=3^4\), it follows that
\[
\log 81=\log(3^4)=4\log3>4.
\]
As \(p\ge81>0\), monotonicity of the logarithm gives
\[
\log p\ge\log81>4.
\]
Both sides here are nonnegative, and the square-root function is strictly increasing on nonnegative numbers. Therefore
\[
\sqrt{\log p}>\sqrt4=2.
\]
This contradicts the inequality \(\sqrt{\log p}\le a(p)=2\) obtained from the conjecture.

Thus the claimed eventual bound already fails for \(\epsilon=1/2\): no matter how large a proposed threshold \(N\) is, a prime \(p\ge\max\{N,81\}\) satisfies
\[
a(p)=2<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1-1/2}.
\]
Hence it is false that for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).
